raw_case_text: We report a case of a 56-year-old man presenting acute fever, cutaneous rash, conjunctival hyperemia, intense joint pain, and self-reported use of non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAID) in the initial days of symptoms. The patient reported that for the last 30 days before Hospital admission, he started presenting fever, headaches, paresthesia, and pain in the right arm with visible red spots on the skin. These skin lesions worsened and spread through the lower limbs and trunk within a period of 10 days. The patient evolved to hypotension with some Hospital admissions and discharges. On the 15th day after skin disease onset, he developed thrombocytopenia, liver dysfunction with International Normalized Ratio (INR) of 1.45 and Prothrombin Time of 56%, edema in his hands and feet and hemorrhagic bullous lesions on the skin of the upper and lower limbs (Figures 1a-c), being admitted to the Intensive Care Unit. Immediately, therapy was started with meropenem and vancomycin, then maintained for 6 days, during which the patient presented some febrile peaks. Subsequently, intravenous administration of Intravenous Immunoglobulin (Human), 5% (Flebogamma  5% DIF, Instituto Grifols S.A., Barcelona, Spain) at 400 mg/Kg/day restarted for 5 days. Antibiotic therapy started again for 5 days. The patient showed a progressive increase in platelet levels from 43,000 to 201,000 and total leukocyte count, together with an important reductions of the edema, necrosis, and erythema. Ten days after globulin administration, a substantial improvement of the bullous lesions was observed (Figures 1g-l). The patient evolved with aphasia, thus being considered to be suffering a transient acute ischemic stroke. Laboratory analysis followed the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) recommendations, in which a single anti-CHIKV IgM-positive test (collected during acute or convalescence phase) is sufficient for confirmation of any suspected case of CHIKV. The blood test returned positive serology for Dengue (IgM-/IgG+) and Chikungunya (IgM+) at the 16th day after symptom onset, but results were negative for other infectious diseases and blood culture. Notably, laboratory tests excluded other confounding diseases such as: malaria, leptospirosis, rheumatic fever, septic arthritis, Zika, and Mayaro. Moreover, there is no report showing any Mayaro case detected in the state of Paraiba. This would definitively exclude the possibility of a cross-reactive IgM serology against another alphavirus as discussed elsewhere. No comorbidities were reported, except for alcoholism. Throughout hospitalization, imaging exams were normal and no vasoactive drugs were administered. Furthermore, no lesions were observed in oral, genital, or conjunctival mucosa. Nikolsky's sign was positive. A diagnosis of Stevens Johnson syndrome-Toxic epidermal necrolysis-like features was discarded. The patient was discharged and has not presented any other clinical sign of the disease.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 56-year-old man presented with a 30-day history of acute fever, headaches, intense arthralgia, conjunctival hyperemia, right arm pain and paresthesias, and progressive erythematous skin lesions evolving into generalized hemorrhagic bullous lesions with acral edema and hypotension.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Thirty days prior to intensive care admission, the patient developed acute fever, headaches, intense joint pain, conjunctival hyperemia, right arm pain and paresthesias, and erythematous skin spots after self-medicating with non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) during the initial days of illness. Over the subsequent 10 days, the cutaneous lesions worsened and spread to the lower limbs and trunk, accompanied by hypotension and multiple hospital admissions and discharges. On day 15 after skin disease onset, he developed hand and foot edema, extensive hemorrhagic bullous skin lesions over the upper and lower extremities, thrombocytopenia, and hepatic dysfunction, prompting admission to the Intensive Care Unit (ICU).
subjective.past_medical_history: History of alcoholism; no other chronic comorbidities reported. Resident of Paraiba state, Brazil.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for fever, headaches, intense arthralgia, conjunctival hyperemia, right arm pain and paresthesias, spreading skin rash with hemorrhagic bullae, and hand/foot edema. Self-medicated with NSAIDs at symptom onset.

objective.physical_examination: Hypotension, edema of the hands and feet, extensive hemorrhagic bullous lesions, erythema, and cutaneous necrosis on the upper and lower extremities with a positive Nikolsky's sign, and conjunctival hyperemia. No lesions were present on the oral, genital, or conjunctival mucosa. During hospitalization, the patient developed transient aphasia.
objective.routine_investigations: On day 15 of skin disease, laboratory testing showed severe thrombocytopenia (platelet count 43,000/mm3, subsequently rising to 201,000/mm3 after treatment), leukocytosis, and liver dysfunction with coagulopathy (INR 1.45, prothrombin time 56%). Imaging studies performed during hospitalization were normal.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Severe acute chikungunya virus (CHIKV) infection presenting with extensive vesiculobullous/hemorrhagic cutaneous lesions, thrombocytopenia, hepatic dysfunction, and transient acute ischemic stroke (aphasia). Serologic testing on day 16 of symptoms (per PAHO criteria) was positive for anti-CHIKV IgM and anti-dengue IgG (dengue IgM negative), while blood cultures and diagnostic tests for Zika virus, Mayaro virus, malaria, leptospirosis, rheumatic fever, and septic arthritis were all negative; Stevens-Johnson syndrome/toxic epidermal necrolysis-like drug reaction was clinically excluded given absence of mucosal involvement. The patient was treated in the ICU with intravenous meropenem and vancomycin (6 days initially, followed by an additional 5-day course) and 5% human intravenous immunoglobulin (Flebogamma 5% DIF, 400 mg/kg/day for 5 days) without requiring vasoactive agents. Within 10 days of IVIG administration, platelet counts normalized (from 43,000 to 201,000/mm3) with marked regression of bullous lesions, edema, necrosis, and erythema, and he was discharged home with complete clinical recovery.
